abstract: Robotic arc welding produces defects that are costly to detect reliably, yet no public benchmark couples the four sensing streams of a production cell (post-weld imaging, in-process video, audio, and process telemetry) with fine-grained, per-class labels. We address this with a benchmark rather than a new architecture. On the Intel Robotic Welding data we define the first supervised four-modality, seven-class defect-classification task under a session-disjoint evaluation protocol, and release MAAF-Net (Multimodal Augmentation-Assisted Fusion Network) with early-, late-, and flat-fusion baselines. Across five seeds MAAF-Net reaches 96.15% test macro-𝐹1 (session-level 95% confidence interval [95.4, 96.8]) with near-saturated binary detection. Because the fixed test split is favourably composed for the minority class and benefits from fold-ensembling and test-time augmentation, we take the multi-seed cross-validation estimate (91.99%) as the more representative figure; there, every configuration lies within seed noise. A sample-level split, as used by the only prior work on this data, inflates that estimate by 7.7 percentage points, motivating our session-disjoint protocol. The only component with a measurable effect is a training-time modality-perturbation curriculum. It leaves clean accuracy within seed noise, yet recovers up to 21.6 percentage points of macro-𝐹1 when two modalities fail together, at no inference cost; the gain persists on held-out corruptions. Neither a composite loss nor an alternative fusion topology improves on plain cross-entropy and hierarchical fusion beyond seed noise. We release the protocol, splits, and baselines; MAAF-Net runs in real time on a single mid-range GPU.
title: A Supervised Multimodal Benchmark and Missing-Modality Robustness Study for Robotic Welding Defect Classification
